rows.title: Ikea Reaches $46 Million Settlement Over Death Of Toddler Killed By Dresser Tip-Over
rows.standfirst: Jozef Dudek was 2 when an Ikea dresser fell on top of him and killed him. His family sued the furniture giant in a wrongful death lawsuit. Millions of the recalled dressers may still be in use.

rows.title: All The Single Ladies...Are Losing In The Housing Market
rows.standfirst: A home is the largest purchase most Americans will ever make. Why single women are losing out in both buying and selling compared to their male counterparts.

rows.title: Economics Still Has A Diversity Problem
rows.standfirst: Despite decades of work, there's been little or no progress on increasing diversity in economics.

rows.title: What's Next In Tech? We Dodged Robots At CES To Find Out
rows.standfirst: At the annual Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, the gadgets range from big-screen TVs and 5G networks to futuristic health care devices and toilet-paper-toting robots.

rows.title: The Business Behind The Color Of The Year
rows.standfirst: Since 2000, the Pantone Color Institute has announced a "color of the year." This year's color: Classic Blue.

rows.title: Investor's Naked Selfies Ignite #MeToo Moment: Female Founder Fights Back
rows.standfirst: Venture capital investing is still a very male-dominated industry where female founders of startups say sexual harassment is a big problem. One woman is trying to change that for herself and others.

rows.title: Life Kit: How To Make Budgeting A Successful New Year's Resolution
rows.standfirst: NPR's Life Kit podcast tackles budgeting and how it might even be an enjoyable New Year's resolution.

rows.title: Mumbai Takes Its Vintage Padmini Taxis Off The Road For Good
rows.standfirst: Residents of India's big financial city hail the end of an era as their classic black and yellow cabs ride off into the sunset.

rows.title: Uber, Lyft, Postmates Refuse To Comply With California Gig Economy Law
rows.standfirst: The new law, which went into effect Wednesday, affects Uber and Lyft drivers as well as journalism freelancers and others. Companies are trying to figure out how to comply or how work around the law.

rows.title: The Skyrocketing Cost Of Air Ambulances
rows.standfirst: After a catastrophic accident, you may be rushed to the hospital in an air ambulance. It could save your life, but there's no way to predict how much it will cost.

rows.title: Oil Prices Reflect Concern, Not Panic, After Airstrike On Iranian General
rows.standfirst: Global oil prices rose by about 4% — a modest increase by historical standards — after the U.S. military killed Qassem Soleimani, the leader of Iran's Quds Force, in an airstrike in Baghdad.

rows.title: Interpol Sends Lebanon Notice About Fugitive Auto Exec Carlos Ghosn
rows.standfirst: The notification is a request to law enforcement to locate and hold the former head of Nissan, who jumped bail in Japan, where he faces financial misconduct charges.

rows.title: The Bubble That Broke Kuwait
rows.standfirst: How a simple financial innovation turned a parking garage in Kuwait into one of the most important markets in the world... and how it all came crashing down.

rows.title: Study: Tinder, Grindr And Other Apps Share Sensitive Personal Data With Advertisers
rows.standfirst: Researchers in Norway say the data-sharing appears to violate European data privacy laws. In the U.S., groups are asking state and federal regulators to investigate whether the practices are illegal.

rows.title: Foxconn's Promises Slow To Materialize In Wisconsin
rows.standfirst: Foxconn was touted as part of a new revival in U.S. manufacturing, and state officials offered nearly $4 billion to lure the company to Wisconsin. Things haven't gone quite as planned.

rows.title: World's Largest Asset Manager Puts Climate At The Center Of Its Investment Strategy
rows.standfirst: "We believe that sustainability should be our new standard for investing," BlackRock CEO Larry Fink says. The investment giant's move puts pressure on companies to reduce reliance on fossil fuels.

rows.title: How Amazon's Counterfeit Products Threaten Safety
rows.standfirst: Over half of sales on Amazon are from third-party sellers, some of whom are selling counterfeit goods. Faulty car seats are threatening children's safety, but is Amazon being held liable?

rows.title: FDA Approves Drugs Faster Than Ever But Relies On Weaker Evidence, Researchers Find
rows.standfirst: Changes in the way the Food and Drug Administration reviews new medicines means that there are more cures and treatments on the market. But there's also less proof the drugs are safe and effective.

rows.title: Moving Beyond GDP
rows.standfirst: After 75 years, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis is developing alternative measures of economic well-being.

rows.title: Hopi Look To Tourism, Ranching For Income After Coal Power Plant Closure
rows.standfirst: The coal power plant that provided about 80% of the Hopi Nation's budget closed last month. Tribal leaders are now trying to figure out how to replace the revenue, which was their economic lifeline.

rows.title: Emotional Currency
rows.standfirst: What's the point of money? The answer might seem obvious: we need it to get paid for our work, and to buy the things we need. But there's also a deeper way to look at the role of money in our lives. This week we explore an anthropologist's take on the origin story of money. What if the cash and coins we carry are not just tools for transactions, but manifestations of human relationships?

rows.title: China To Test Digital Currency. Could It End Up Challenging The Dollar Globally?
rows.standfirst: Bitcoin promises users anonymity, but transactions using China's digital currency would be tracked by its central bank. Experts say it could someday rival the dollar in international payments.

rows.title: How Trade Wars Fill The Swamp
rows.standfirst: How lobbyists' campaigns for exclusions to the trade war have skewed incentives and disadvantaged small businesses.

rows.title: Former Export-Import Bank Chairman On How 'Trade Is Not A Four-Letter Word'
rows.standfirst: NPR's Ari Shapiro talks with Fred Hochberg, former chair of the Export-Import Bank, about his book Trade Is Not a Four-Letter Word: How Six Everyday Products Make the Case for Trade.

rows.title: As New CEO Takes Charge, Boeing's Challenges Remain
rows.standfirst: Boeing's new CEO David Calhoun has served on the company's board of directors since 2009, leading some to worry he can't bring an outsider's perspective and shake things up.

rows.title: Pharmaceutical Executives Face Prison Time In Case Linked To Opioid Crisis
rows.standfirst: John Kapoor, the former billionaire who founded drugmaker Insys Therapeutics, is among the executives to be sentenced for racketeering.

rows.title: The Kratom Debate: Helpful Herb Or Dangerous Drug?
rows.standfirst: Some people struggling with opioid addiction who switched to kratom swear the herb salvaged their lives. But federal agencies and the brother of a man who died from his kratom use warn of its risks.

rows.title: Australia's Massive Fires Threaten To Slow Decades-Long Economic Boom
rows.standfirst: Australia hasn't had a recession in nearly 30 years, an impressive track record for an industrialized county. But the fires threaten two pillars of the country's economy.

rows.title: Boeing 737 Max May Stay Grounded Into Summer
rows.standfirst: Boeing suggests it could fly about mid-2020. Industry sources note that the FAA and other regulators around the world could take months longer to find the planes safe to fly passengers.

rows.title: Can You Name Five Fine Artists That Are Women?
rows.standfirst: On average, work by women artists sells for 40% less than work by male artists. Their work also represents just a small sliver of what's displayed in museums. So, how did women get shut out of the art world?

rows.title: Law Enforcement Officials Argue Rural Homeless Services Worsen Problem
rows.standfirst: Rural homelessness in Oregon isn't as visible as its urban equivalent, but it's a major problem. Even when money is available, local officials say providing resources could make the problem worse.

rows.title: The Story Of Money: How Human Behavior Shapes Economies — And Vice Versa
rows.standfirst: What's the point of money? The answer might seem obvious: we need it to get paid for our work, and to buy the things we need. But there's also a deeper way to look at the role of money in our lives.

rows.title: More Data On The Midlife Crisis
rows.standfirst: An economist uses a broad range of data from 132 countries to understand why middle age is such a drag.

rows.title: Iran Conflict Could Shift To Cyberspace, Experts Warn
rows.standfirst: After the U.S. killed Iran's top military leader, government officials and security experts say Iran could retaliate with cyberattacks ranging from destroying data to defacing websites.

rows.title: Extradition Trial For Huawei Executive Facing U.S. Fraud Charges Begins In Vancouver
rows.standfirst: Meng Wanzhou was arrested in 2018 as she changed planes in Vancouver. The U.S. says the Chinese technology giant misled banks about the nature of Huawei's business in Iran.

rows.title: Patients Still Struggle To Balance High Costs Of MS Treatment, Despite Generic
rows.standfirst: Drugs to treat multiple sclerosis can run $70,000 a year or more. Patients hoped competition from a generic version of one of the most popular brands would spur relief, but prices went up. Here's why.

rows.title: Does The China Trade Deal Move The World Away From Free Trade?
rows.standfirst: While the new deal with China lowers some trade barriers, it leaves many tariffs in place. And it dictates that China buy more from the U.S., but that has other trading partners worried.

rows.title: Elk Raise Tensions Between Tribes And Farmers In Washington's Skagit Valley
rows.standfirst: In Washington state's Skagit Valley, a conflict is unfolding between Native Americans and farmers. Elk are making a comeback there. Local tribes are thrilled, but the agriculture industry is not.

rows.title: Meals On Wheels Serves Up Breakfast, Lunch And Community At Local Diner
rows.standfirst: Meals on Wheels usually means home delivery or lunch at a senior center. But at a new project in Vancouver, Wash., it's a retro-hip neighborhood diner where seniors can get eggs, coffee and community.

rows.title: Amtrak Asks 2 People Who Use Wheelchairs To Pay $25,000 For A Ride
rows.standfirst: It usually costs $16 to take Amtrak from Chicago to Bloomington, Ill. The company defended the $25,000 cost for the extra wheelchair users, saying it reflects a new policy.

rows.title: A Bag of Bolívares: And Other Indicators From Venezuela
rows.standfirst: Venezuela started 2019 with rolling blackouts, hyperinflation, and crippling food shortages. Things have actually gotten a little better, mostly thanks to the economic innovations of everyday people.

rows.title: The Cost Of Free: Casper Pays A Price For Generous Mattress Returns
rows.standfirst: Casper changed mattress shopping with the promise of a 100-night "risk-free" trial and easy returns. Now the cost of those returns is being scrutinized as the online company prepares to go public.

rows.title: In China, Birthrate Falls To Lowest Level In 70 Years
rows.standfirst: Last year, there were 10.48 births per 1,000 people — the lowest since the country was founded in 1949. Beijing also said its economy cooled to the slowest pace in nearly three decades.

rows.title: A Business Owner's View On Brexit
rows.standfirst: Today is Brexit Day. As of 11:00pm tonight (GMT), the UK will no longer be part of the European Union. We spoke to a small business owner about what that might mean.

rows.title: The Hummer Is Coming Back — As An Electric Vehicle
rows.standfirst: In the early 2000s, the Hummer was a symbol of gas-guzzling militaristic excess. Now it's getting revived as an electric pickup. It's one sign of how much things have changed in the auto industry.

rows.title: Education Dept. Unveils Fix For Student Loan Program's 'Bureaucratic Nightmare'
rows.standfirst: In its first year, the forgiveness program turned away 71% of borrowers because of a paperwork technicality. Now, the department says it's fixing that roadblock.

rows.title: White House Moves To Formally Decriminalize Accidentally Killing Birds
rows.standfirst: Wildlife protection groups are decrying the proposal as an attempt to gut a century-old law that protects birds, while industry groups say they have long been hamstrung by the threat of legal action.

rows.title: Senators To CFPB: Why Are You Still Failing To Protect Student Loan Borrowers?
rows.standfirst: Democratic lawmakers sent a letter to the director of the nation's top consumer watchdog agency demanding that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau do its job supervising the student loan system.

rows.title: American Dynamism In Decline
rows.standfirst: America has a hard-earned reputation for being the most dynamic economy on the globe. But that dynamism could be waning.

rows.title: FICO Is About To Change Credit Scores. Here's Why It Matters
rows.standfirst: The firm says 40 million Americans' scores will drop by more than 20 points, and a similar number will rise.

rows.title: U.S. Economic Growth Slowed In 2019 To 2.3%
rows.standfirst: The Commerce Department says the U.S. economy grew 2.3% last year. That's slower than the previous year and well below the Trump administration's forecast.

rows.title: In Battle For Europe's Phones, U.S. Suffers Setback, Huawei Notches A Win
rows.standfirst: In U.S. national security, one foreign company sets off alarm bells like no other: Huawei, the telecom giant. The Chinese firm just received a green light to help build Britain's 5G cellular network.

rows.title: The Economic Impact Of An Infectious Disease
rows.standfirst: As the coronavirus spreads internationally, we wanted to know what it looks like when an infectious disease shuts down one of the world's largest economies. We speak with NPR Beijing correspondent, Emily Feng.

rows.title: Starbucks Closes More Than 2,000 Stores In China Amid Coronavirus Outbreak
rows.standfirst: The coffee chain has temporarily closed the stores locations to limit the spread of the coronavirus that has sickened more than 4,500 people.

rows.title: Weird (Amazon) Flex, But Okay
rows.standfirst: Nearly half of Amazon's packages are delivered not by UPS or USPS, but by the company itself. Amazon employs thousands of gig workers to make its deliveries, administering them through an app called Amazon Flex.

rows.title: Due To New California Law, Uber Allows Some Drivers To Set Their Own Rates
rows.standfirst: The experiment underway at three airports comes in reaction to a recent state law that makes it harder to classify people as contract workers rather than as employees.

rows.title: I Can't Work With You! How Political Fights Leave Workplaces Divided
rows.standfirst: Amid impeachment and the 2020 election, surveys show political fevers running high at work, undercutting trust and productivity. And workers and employers are bracing for those dynamics to get worse.

rows.title: Kobe Bryant's Death Puts A Focus On Helicopter Safety
rows.standfirst: Some helicopter trips — like personal or private helicopter rides — are more likely than others to end in a fatal accident. A crash killed the former NBA star and eight other people on Sunday.
